stances.claim: Last week, Trump issued a stark warning to Iran via social media -- 'a whole civilization [would] die tonight, never to be brought back again' if Tehran failed to meet his deadline. Shortly after, a two-week ceasefire was announced alongside Iran's reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for roughly one-fifth of global oil/gas trade. As of writing, the ceasefire remains at risk due to alleged US-Israel violations striking Lebanon and Iran refusing to reopen Hormuz.

UN Spokesperson Stephane Dujarric expressed alarm at Trump's rhetoric, noting threats to target civilian infrastructure, if acted upon, could risk violating international humanitarian law. The UN Charter Article 2(4) commands all member states -- including the US, Israel, Iran, and others -- to 'refrain ... from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.' As a founding member of the UN and a permanent UNSC member, the US did not merely sign this document; its leaders wrote it. That pledge carries weight beyond politics -- it represents a commitment, forged from the ashes of two world wars, to replace the law of the jungle with the rule of law.
stances.rhetorical_move: Dujarric-alarm + UN-Charter-Article-2(4) verbatim + US-wrote-it + replace-law-of-jungle-with-rule-of-law framing

stances.claim: Clearly, the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran and the killing of its leaders were conducted without full congressional approval, without UNSC authorization, and without evidence of an imminent armed attack to justify the inherent right to self-defense under Article 51. Even if the US were to claim legitimate self-defense, the methods of warfare must still comply with the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their protocols. Threatening to leave 'every power plant and bridge in Iran burning, exploding, and never to be used again' is not battlefield bluster -- it is a direct challenge to the principle of distinction under the laws of war, differentiating at all times between military targets and civilian infrastructure.
stances.rhetorical_move: triple-procedural-violation (no-Congress + no-UNSC + no-imminent-attack) + Geneva-Conventions + principle-of-distinction framing

stances.claim: The consequences were swift and destabilizing -- retaliatory risks escalated; Hormuz disruption sent shock waves through global markets; US allies withheld support, with many refusing to endorse what they characterized as an illegitimate use of force. History offers a sobering lesson for those who mistake military audacity for strategic wisdom -- Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor was designed as a decisive blow, but it merely served to ignite American patriotism to change US neutrality to militant unity to defend the motherland. Russia's invasion of Ukraine has devolved into a grinding war of attrition marked by casualties, isolation, and economic sanctions.

UN Sec-Gen António Guterres, echoing the General Assembly sentiment, has condemned the surprise attack on Iran as a UN-Charter violation. CJP doubts, however, whether the UNSC -- in which the US has veto power -- can use coercive authority to stop the attack and restore status quo ante. Sad indeed is the situation when a major power is the violator of the UN Charter and laws of war -- UN's peace mandates cannot be enforced. While holding the presidency, Trump -- being constitutionally immune like any incumbent Philippine president -- cannot be tried/convicted in US courts; waiting for term-expiration or impeachment may be too late. Not even the ICC can enforce its arrest orders, if any are issued, on Trump -- same way it could not on Putin.

Verily, enforcement of UN majorities against a major power like the US remains a pipe dream -- the ICJ judicial organ faces limits in disputes involving permanent UNSC members; Geneva Conventions enforcement on the laws of war cannot be observed. However, accountability is not only judicial -- it is political, historical, diplomatic, and democratic. Recent polls show measurable decline in Trump's domestic approval, revealing deepening divisions over both human costs and strategic direction. The reluctance of key US allies, especially European, to lend support constitutes a broader international verdict.
stances.rhetorical_move: judicial-enforcement-pipe-dream + four-fold-accountability (political + historical + diplomatic + democratic) + polls-and-allies international-verdict

stances.claim: Violating the UN Charter while expecting other nations to absorb the consequences is not leadership; it is unilateralism that corrodes the very architecture of collective security. The world cannot afford another precedent where might makes right, where powerful states selectively honor the rules they helped create. The international community has arrived at a crossroads -- one path leads toward a rules-based order, however imperfect; the other leads toward a world where power alone defines legitimacy, and where no nation, however strong today, is safe tomorrow. The rule of law is not merely a preference. It remains the ultimate arbiter.

notable_anecdotes: The 'a whole civilization [would] die tonight, never to be brought back again' Trump-social-media quotation -- among the most extreme apocalyptic-threat rhetoric ever quoted in CJP's column corpus, deliberately reproduced to anchor the international-humanitarian-law analysis.

The 'every power plant and bridge in Iran burning, exploding, and never to be used again' Trump-threat captured as direct-challenge to principle-of-distinction -- using verbatim civilian-infrastructure-targeting language to ground the laws-of-war violation analysis.

The Pearl Harbor historical-analogue -- captured as anti-decisive-blow lesson: 'designed as a decisive blow, but it merely served to ignite American patriotism' -- turning the typical US-victim-of-surprise-attack narrative into a cautionary tale against US-as-surprise-attacker.

The Russia-Ukraine 'grinding war of attrition' framing -- captures the contemporary parallel to Pearl Harbor's lesson, with 'casualties, isolation, and economic sanctions' as the predictable outcomes of unilateral aggression.
The 'US did not merely sign this document; its leaders wrote it' framing on UN Charter -- among CJP's most pointed framings of US-as-architect-now-violator of post-WWII international legal order.
The 'replace the law of the jungle with the rule of law' framing -- captures the foundational postwar-international-order project in a single phrase.

The Trump-immunity-parallel-to-incumbent-PH-president comparison -- CJP applying his own constitutional-jurisprudence expertise to the US case, demonstrating cross-jurisdictional consistency on sitting-executive immunity.

The ICC-Putin-parallel-for-Trump observation -- among CJP's tightest captures of judicial-enforcement-against-major-powers asymmetry, predicting (correctly) that ICC has no enforcement mechanism against US-permanent-member-protected leadership.

The 'accountability is not only judicial. It is political, historical, diplomatic, and democratic' four-fold reformulation -- among CJP's most important contributions to the international-law-against-major-powers debate: redirecting accountability discourse from blocked-judicial venues to multi-track non-judicial accountability paths.

The 'might makes right ... where no nation, however strong today, is safe tomorrow' formulation -- a Thucydidean realism warning embedded in a rule-of-law column, captured as the natural endpoint of unilateral-precedent normalization.

The 'rule of law is not merely a preference. It remains the ultimate arbiter' closing -- CJP's most condensed normative-claim closing in his Trump-accountability arc, denying the realist-might-equals-right framing in the strongest available terms.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban interrogates how the international community can hold the US and President Donald Trump accountable for unilateral action against Iran. Last week, Trump issued a stark warning to Iran via social media -- 'a whole civilization [would] die tonight, never to be brought back again' if Tehran failed to meet his deadline. Shortly after, a two-week ceasefire was announced alongside Iran's reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for roughly one-fifth of global oil/gas trade. As of writing, the ceasefire remains at risk -- alleged US-Israel violations striking Lebanon and Iran refusing to reopen Hormuz. UN Spokesperson Stephane Dujarric expressed alarm at Trump's rhetoric, noting threats to target civilian infrastructure could risk violating international humanitarian law. UN Charter Article 2(4) commands all member states -- including the US, Israel, Iran, and others -- to 'refrain ... from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.' As a founding member of the UN and permanent UNSC member, the US did not merely sign this document; its leaders wrote it -- a commitment forged from the ashes of two world wars to replace the law of the jungle with the rule of law. Clearly, the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran and the killing of its leaders were conducted without full congressional approval, without UNSC authorization, and without evidence of an imminent armed attack justifying Article 51 self-defense. Even if the US claimed legitimate self-defense, the methods must still comply with the 1949 Geneva Conventions and protocols. Threatening to leave 'every power plant and bridge in Iran burning, exploding, and never to be used again' is not battlefield bluster -- it is a direct challenge to the principle of distinction under the laws of war, differentiating military targets from civilian infrastructure. Consequences were swift and destabilizing -- retaliatory risks escalated; Hormuz disruption sent shock waves through global markets; US allies withheld support, many refusing to endorse what they characterized as illegitimate use of force. History offers a sobering lesson for those who mistake military audacity for strategic wisdom: Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor was designed as a decisive blow, but merely served to ignite American patriotism, changing US neutrality to militant unity. Russia's invasion of Ukraine has devolved into a grinding war of attrition marked by casualties, isolation, and economic sanctions. UN Sec-Gen António Guterres, echoing the General Assembly, condemned the surprise attack on Iran as UN-Charter violation -- but the UNSC, in which the US has veto power, cannot use its coercive authority to stop the attack and restore status quo ante. Sad indeed is the situation when a major power violates the UN Charter and laws of war -- UN's peace mandates cannot be enforced. While holding the presidency, Trump -- being constitutionally immune, like any incumbent Philippine president -- cannot be tried in US courts; waiting for term-expiration or impeachment may be too late. Not even the ICC can enforce its arrest orders, if any are issued, on Trump -- same way it could not on Russia's Putin. Verily, enforcement of UN majorities against a major power like the US remains a pipe dream -- the ICJ faces limits in permanent-member disputes; Geneva Conventions enforcement cannot be observed. However, accountability is not only judicial. It is political, historical, diplomatic, and democratic. Recent polls show measurable decline in Trump's domestic approval, revealing deepening divisions over human costs and strategic direction. The reluctance of key US allies, especially European, constitutes a broader international verdict. Violating the UN Charter while expecting other nations to absorb the consequences is not leadership; it is unilateralism that corrodes the very architecture of collective security. The world cannot afford another precedent where might makes right, where powerful states selectively honor the rules they helped create. The international community has arrived at a crossroads -- one path leads toward a rules-based order, however imperfect; the other leads toward a world where power alone defines legitimacy, and where no nation, however strong today, is safe tomorrow. The rule of law is not merely a preference. It remains the ultimate arbiter.
